recording | description = Performed by the Toyama Army School Military Band | filename2 = Kimi ga Yo (Fenton).mid | title2 = MIDI version of Fenton's original (melody only) | filename3 = | title3 = Fenton's original with orchestral instruments }} {{nihongo|"'''Kimigayo'''"|}} is the {{ill|national anthem|en|national anthem|WD=Q23691|lt=national anthem|1=National anthem}} of {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. The lyrics are from a ''{{translit|ja|{{ill|Waka (poetry)|en|Waka (poetry)|WD=Q737148|lt=waka|1=Waka (poetry)}}}}'' poem written by an unnamed author in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}} (794–1185),{{cite web |url=http://nationalanthems.me/japan-kimigayo|title=Japan – Kimigayo |publisher=NationalAnthems.me|access-date=2011-11-28|url-status=dead|archive-date=2011-12-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111227000629/http://nationalanthems.me/japan-kimigayo/}} and the current melody was chosen in 1880,{{cite web|url=http://www.national-anthems.org/facts.htm|title=Facts About National Anthems|website=www.national-anthems.org|access-date=2023-03-23|archive-date=2017-10-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171012160352/http://www.national-anthems.org/facts.htm|url-status=live}} The music of the {{ill|Netherlands|en|Netherlands|WD=Q55|lt=Dutch|1=Netherlands}} anthem {{ill|Wilhelmus|en|Wilhelmus|WD=Q131713|lt=Wilhelmus|1=Wilhelmus}} was composed in 1568. replacing an unpopular melody composed by {{ill|John William Fenton|en|John William Fenton|WD=Q3182754|lt=John William Fenton|1=John William Fenton}} in 1869. While the title "Kimigayo" is usually translated as "{{ill|Imperial Majesty|en|Imperial Majesty|WD=Q6006744|lt=His Imperial Majesty|1=Imperial Majesty}}'s Reign", no official translation of the title or lyrics have been established in law.{{cite news |date=2008-03-29 |title=Elementary schools face new mandate: Patriotism, 'Kimigayo' |work={{ill|The Japan Times|en|The Japan Times|WD=Q1190886|lt=The Japan Times|1=The Japan Times}} Online |agency=Kyodo News |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2008/03/29/national/elementary-schools-face-new-mandate-patriotism-kimigayo/ |access-date=2011-08-20 |url-access=subscription |archive-date=2015-05-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150503113855/http://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2008/03/29/national/elementary-schools-face-new-mandate-patriotism-kimigayo/ |url-status=live }} From 1888 to 1945, "Kimigayo" served as the national anthem of the {{ill|Empire of Japan|en|Empire of Japan|WD=Q188712|lt=Empire of Japan|1=Empire of Japan}}. When the Empire was dissolved following {{ill|Surrender of Japan|en|Surrender of Japan|WD=Q6540361|lt=its surrender|1=Surrender of Japan}} at the end of [[World War II]], the new state of Japan succeeded it in 1947. This {{ill|successor state|en|successor state|WD=Q1054283|lt=successor state|1=Successor state}} was a {{ill|Parliamentary system|en|Parliamentary system|WD=Q166747|lt=parliamentary democracy|1=Parliamentary system}}, {{ill|Constitutional monarchy|en|Constitutional monarchy|WD=Q41614|lt=Constitutional monarchy|1=Constitutional monarchy}} and the {{ill|Polity|en|Polity|WD=Q1063239|lt=Polity|1=Polity}} therefore changed from a system based on imperial {{ill|Sovereignty|en|Sovereignty|WD=Q42008|lt=Sovereignty|1=Sovereignty}} to one based on {{ill|Popular sovereignty|en|Popular sovereignty|WD=Q285950|lt=Popular sovereignty|1=Popular sovereignty}}. However, the {{ill|Occupation of Japan|en|Occupation of Japan|WD=Q696251|lt=Allied occupation|1=Occupation of Japan}} forces (mainly {{ill|United States Armed Forces|en|United States Armed Forces|WD=Q11211|lt=U.S. military|1=United States Armed Forces}}) allowed {{ill|Hirohito|en|Hirohito|WD=Q34479|lt=Hirohito|1=Hirohito}}, Emperor Shōwa to retain the throne and "Kimigayo" remained the ''{{ill|De facto|en|De facto|WD=Q712144|lt=De facto|1=De facto}}'' national anthem for preservation of {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Japanese monarchy|1=Emperor of Japan}}. The passage of the {{ill|Act on National Flag and Anthem|en|Act on National Flag and Anthem|WD=Q3270407|lt=Act on National Flag and Anthem|1=Act on National Flag and Anthem}} in 1999 recognised it as the official national and imperial anthem. == Etymology == "''Kimi''" has been used to indicate the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor of Japan|1=Emperor of Japan}} or one's lord (i.e., master) since at least the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}.新村出記念財団(1998). A dictionary of {{ill|Japanese language|en|Japanese language|WD=Q5287|lt=language|1=Japanese language}} 『広辞苑』 ("''Kōjien''"), 5th edition. Published by [http://www.iwanami.co.jp/ Iwanami Shoten, Publishers] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111007132110/http://iwanami.co.jp/search/index.html |date=2011-10-07 }}.{{cite web |url=http://www.furutasigaku.jp/jfuruta/jwagakim/jwagaki1.html |script-title=ja:君が代の源流 |website=Furuta's Historical Science Association |language=ja |access-date=2008-05-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130529041318/http://www.furutasigaku.jp/jfuruta/jwagakim/jwagaki1.html |archive-date=2013-05-29 }} {{cite web |url=http://www.furutasigaku.jp/efuruta/ewagakim/ewagaki.html |title=Inside "Kimigayo" |access-date=2008-05-10 |website=Furuta's Historical Science Association |archive-date=2023-06-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602215903/https://furutasigaku.jp/efuruta/ewagakim/ewagaki.html |url-status=live }} For example, the protagonist {{Nihongo3||光源氏|{{ill|Hikaru Genji|en|Hikaru Genji|WD=Q997646|lt=Hikaru Genji|1=Hikaru Genji}}}} of ''{{ill|The Tale of Genji|en|The Tale of Genji|WD=Q8269|lt=The Tale of Genji|1=The Tale of Genji}}'' is also called {{Nihongo3||光の君 {{lang|en|or}} 光君|"Hikaru no Kimi" {{lang|en|or|italic=no}} "Hikaru-gimi"}}. Before the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}}, the emperor was often called "''ohkimi''" (great lord); so it is controversial whether or not the word "''kimi''" in "''kimigayo''" had meant "emperor" originally. "Kimi" also means "my dear" as female emperor {{ill|Empress Genmei|en|Empress Genmei|WD=Q233224|lt=Genmei|1=Empress Genmei}} wrote about her lover in a poem in [[:en:Manyoshu|Manyoshu]] (vol.1 no.78). In the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}, "Kimigayo" was used as a festive song among {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai|1=Samurai}}, and then became popular among the people in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}. In the later part of the Edo period, "Kimigayo" was used in the {{ill|Ōoku|en|Ōoku|WD=Q1064983|lt=Ōoku|1=Ōoku}} (harem of {{ill|Edo Castle|en|Edo Castle|WD=Q865913|lt=Edo Castle|1=Edo Castle}}, current [[Tokyo Imperial Palace]]) and {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma-han|1=Satsuma Domain}} (current {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture|1=Kagoshima Prefecture}}) as a common festive new year song. In those contexts, "''kimi''" never meant the emperor, but only the [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa shōgun]], the {{ill|Shimazu clan|en|Shimazu clan|WD=Q1061406|lt=Shimazu clan|1=Shimazu clan}} as rulers of the Satsuma-han, guests of honor, or all members of a festive drinking party. After the [[Meiji Restoration]], samurai from Satsuma-han controlled the Imperial Japanese government, and they adopted "Kimigayo" as the national anthem of Japan. From this time until the {{ill|Surrender of Japan|en|Surrender of Japan|WD=Q6540361|lt=Japanese defeat|1=Surrender of Japan}} at the {{ill|End of World War II in Asia|en|End of World War II in Asia|WD=Q5375854|lt=end of World War II|1=End of World War II in Asia}}, "Kimigayo" was understood to mean the long reign of the Emperor. With the adoption of the {{ill|Constitution of Japan|en|Constitution of Japan|WD=Q237082|lt=Constitution of Japan|1=Constitution of Japan}} in 1947, the Emperor became no longer a {{ill|Head of state|en|Head of state|WD=Q48352|lt=sovereign|1=Head of state}} who ruled by {{ill|Divine right of kings|en|Divine right of kings|WD=Q839452|lt=divine right|1=Divine right of kings}}, but a human who is a symbol of the state and of the unity of the people as a constitutional monarch.{{cite book |editor=Michael Williams |editor2=Graham Humphrys |title=Citizenship Education and Lifelong Learning: Power and Place |publisher=Nova Biomedical Books |year=2003 |page=126 |isbn=978-1-59033-863-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FrwMHKDPUzQC&q=kimigayo&pg=PA126 |access-date=2020-10-18 |archive-date=2024-02-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240229221402/https://books.google.com/books?id=FrwMHKDPUzQC&q=kimigayo&pg=PA126#v=snippet&q=kimigayo&f=false |url-status=live }} The {{ill|Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology|en|Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology|WD=Q1054379|lt=Ministry of Education|1=Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology}} did not give any new meanings for "Kimigayo" after the war; this allowed the song to mean the Japanese people. The Ministry also did not formally renounce the pre-war meaning of "Kimigayo".{{cite book|title=Nationalism: Critical concepts in political science|isbn=978-0-415-21756-9|last1=Hutchinson|first1=John|last2=Smith|first2=Anthony D.|year=2000|publisher=Taylor & Francis|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gUjNKxTrju4C&q=kimigayo&pg=PA1905|access-date=2020-10-18|archive-date=2024-02-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240229221402/https://books.google.com/books?id=gUjNKxTrju4C&q=kimigayo&pg=PA1905#v=snippet&q=kimigayo&f=false|url-status=live}} In 1999, during the deliberations of the {{ill|Act on National Flag and Anthem|en|Act on National Flag and Anthem|WD=Q3270407|lt=Act on National Flag and Anthem|1=Act on National Flag and Anthem}}, the official definition of ''Kimi'' or ''Kimi-ga-yo'' was questioned repeatedly. The first suggestion, which was given by {{ill|Chief Cabinet Secretary|en|Chief Cabinet Secretary|WD=Q1078482|lt=Chief Cabinet Secretary|1=Chief Cabinet Secretary}} {{ill|Hiromu Nonaka|en|Hiromu Nonaka|WD=Q696583|lt=Hiromu Nonaka|1=Hiromu Nonaka}}, stated that ''kimi'' meant the "Emperor as the symbol of Japan", and that the entire lyrics wish for the peace and prosperity of Japan. He referred to the new status of emperor as established in Article 1 of the Constitution of Japan as the main reason for these suggestions.{{cite journal|title=Japan's Neo-Nationalism: The Role of the Hinomaru and Kimigayo Legislation |journal=Japan Policy Research Institute Working Paper|date=July 2001|first=Mayumi|last=Itoh |volume=79 |url= http://www.jpri.org/publications/workingpapers/wp79.html |access-date=2010-10-13|archive-date=2018-10-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181002192508/http://www.jpri.org/publications/workingpapers/wp79.html|url-status=dead}} During the same session, {{ill|Prime Minister of Japan|en|Prime Minister of Japan|WD=Q274948|lt=Prime Minister|1=Prime Minister of Japan}} {{ill|Keizō Obuchi|en|Keizō Obuchi|WD=Q313339|lt=Keizō Obuchi|1=Keizō Obuchi}} ({{ill|Obuchi Cabinet|en|Obuchi Cabinet|WD=Q1530370|lt=Obuchi Cabinet|1=Obuchi cabinet}}) confirmed this meaning with a statement on 29 June 1999:
"''Kimi''" indicates the Emperor, who is the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people, and whose position is derived from the consensus-based will of Japanese citizens, with whom sovereign power resides. And, the phrase "Kimigayo" indicates our State, Japan, which has the Emperor enthroned as the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people by the consensus-based will of Japanese citizens. And it is reasonable to take the lyric of "Kimigayo" to mean the wish for the lasting prosperity and peace of such country of ours.{{cite web |author=The House of Representatives |date=1999-06-29 |url=http://kokkai.ndl.go.jp/SENTAKU/syugiin/145/0001/14506290001041c.html |title=Info of the minutes of the plenary session No.41 of the House of Representatives in the 145th Diet term |language=ja |website=National Diet Library |access-date=2008-05-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080411201108/http://kokkai.ndl.go.jp/SENTAKU/syugiin/145/0001/14506290001041c.html |archive-date=2008-04-11}}
Parties opposed to the {{ill|Liberal Democratic Party (Japan)|en|Liberal Democratic Party (Japan)|WD=Q232595|lt=Liberal Democratic Party|1=Liberal Democratic Party (Japan)}}, which was in control of the government during Obuchi administration, strongly objected to the government's meaning of ''kimi'' and "Kimigayo". Lawmakers of the {{ill|Democratic Party of Japan|en|Democratic Party of Japan|WD=Q200314|lt=Democratic Party of Japan|1=Democratic Party of Japan}} objected on the grounds that there was a lack of any historical ties to the meaning. The strongest critic was {{ill|Kazuo Shii|en|Kazuo Shii|WD=Q337507|lt=Kazuo Shii|1=Kazuo Shii}}, the chairman of the {{ill|Japanese Communist Party|en|Japanese Communist Party|WD=Q641600|lt=Communist Party of Japan|1=Japanese Communist Party}}, who strongly claimed that "Japan" could not be derived from "Kimigayo", because the lyrics only mention wishing for the emperor to have a long reign. Shii also objected to the use of the song as the national anthem, saying that for a democratic nation, an anthem about the emperor was not appropriate. == History == === Empire of Japan (1868–1945) === [[File:Shimogamo-Sazareishi-M1641.jpg|thumb|''Sazare-Ishi'' pebbles are believed to grow into boulders in some legends. A photo taken at [[Kamo shrines|''Shimogamo'' Shrine]] in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyōto|1=Kyoto}}.]] The lyrics first appeared in the {{lang|ja-latn|{{ill|Kokin Wakashū|en|Kokin Wakashū|WD=Q1047167|lt=Kokin Wakashū|1=Kokin Wakashū}}}}, a poetry anthology published in ca.920, as an anonymous poem. The poem was included in many anthologies, and was used in a later period as a celebration song of a long life by people of all social statures. Unlike the form used for the current national anthem, the poem originally began with "''Waga Kimi wa''" ('my lord') instead of "''Kimiga Yo wa''" ('my lord's reign').{{sfn|Goodman|Neary|1996|p=78}} The first lyrics were changed during the Kamakura period, while the rest of the lyrics stayed the same. Because the lyrics were sung on informal occasions, such as birthdays, there was no sheet music for it until the 19th century. In 1869, {{ill|John William Fenton|en|John William Fenton|WD=Q3182754|lt=John William Fenton|1=John William Fenton}}, a visiting British military band leader, realized that there was no national anthem in Japan, and suggested to {{ill|Ōyama Iwao|en|Ōyama Iwao|WD=Q359819|lt=Iwao Ōyama|1=Ōyama Iwao}}, an officer of the [[:en:Satsuma Clan|Satsuma Clan]], that one be created. Ōyama agreed, and selected the lyrics.{{cite web|author=Aura Sabadus |date=2006-03-14|title=Japan searches for Scot who modernised nation|publisher=Johnston Press Digital Publishing |url=http://thescotsman.scotsman.com/index.cfm?id=379822006 |access-date=2007-12-10|archive-url=https://archive.today/20121216103557/http://thescotsman.scotsman.com/index.cfm?id=379822006 |url-status=dead|archive-date=2012-12-16|work=The Scotsman}} The lyrics may have been chosen for their similarity to the [[:en:God Save the Queen|British national anthem]], due to Fenton's influence.{{cite web |author=Colin Joyce |date=2005-08-30 |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/main.jhtml?xml=/news/2005/08/30/wjapan30.xml|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071216065311/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/main.jhtml?xml=%2Fnews%2F2005%2F08%2F30%2Fwjapan30.xml|url-status=dead|archive-date=2007-12-16|title=Briton who gave Japan its anthem |work=telegraph.co.uk|publisher=Telegraph Media Group Limited|access-date=2007-12-10}} After selecting the anthem's lyrics, Ōyama then asked Fenton to create the melody. After being given just two{{cite book|last=Boyd|first=Richard|author2=Tak-Wing Ngo|title=State Making in Asia|publisher=Routledge|year=2006|page=40|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WF-ucX4oywIC&q=kimigayo&pg=PA40|isbn=978-0-415-34611-5|access-date=2020-10-18|archive-date=2024-02-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240229221403/https://books.google.com/books?id=WF-ucX4oywIC&q=kimigayo&pg=PA40|url-status=live}} to three weeks to compose the melody, and only a few days to rehearse, Fenton debuted the anthem before the Japanese Emperor in 1870. This was the first version of "Kimigayo". This was discarded because the melody "lacked solemnity", according to the Japanese government,{{cite web|url=http://web-japan.org/factsheet/en/pdf/11NFlagAnthem.pdf|title=National Flag and Anthem|work=Web Japan|publisher=Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs|year=2000|access-date=2009-12-11|archive-date=2010-06-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100615104013/http://web-japan.org/factsheet/en/pdf/11NFlagAnthem.pdf|url-status=live}} although others believe it is because the melody was actually "unsingable" for the Japanese.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GeasCAAAQBAJ|title=Republic or Death! Travels in Search of National Anthems|last=Marshall|first=Alex|publisher=Windmill Books|year=2016|isbn=978-0-09-959223-5|location=London|page=104|quote=Fenton's effort was overhauled in 1880 because it turned out to be completely unsingable if you were Japanese – 'Japanese is not a tonal language, but it has its highs and lows, and he got it completely wrong, 'Professor Kazuo Fukushima, the director of Japan's Music Historiography Research Institute, told me – but after the rework it grew in prominence, especially as Japan's ruling elite tried to create a modern country...|access-date=2020-10-18|archive-date=2024-02-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240229221456/https://books.google.com/books?id=GeasCAAAQBAJ|url-status=live}} However, this version is still performed annually at the ''Myōkōji'' temple in {{ill|Yokohama|en|Yokohama|WD=Q38283|lt=Yokohama|1=Yokohama}}, where Fenton served as a military band leader. ''Myōkōji'' serves as a memorial to him. [[File:Curt-Netto-Japanese-National-Hymn-Coverdesign-1880.jpg|thumb|upright|left|{{ill|Franz Eckert|en|Franz Eckert|WD=Q569367|lt=Franz Eckert|1=Franz Eckert}}'s notes, presented to the Meiji-Tennō in 1880 (cover design by {{ill|Curt Netto|en|Curt Netto|WD=Q84901|lt=Curt Netto|1=Curt Netto}})]] In 1880, the {{ill|Ministry of the Imperial Household|en|Ministry of the Imperial Household|WD=Q8193428|lt=Ministry of the Imperial Household|1=Ministry of the Imperial Household}} (current {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}}) adopted a new melody composed by Yoshiisa Oku and Akimori Hayashi. The composer is often listed as {{ill|Hiromori Hayashi|en|Hiromori Hayashi|WD=Q3783782|lt=Hiromori Hayashi|1=Hiromori Hayashi}}, who was their supervisor and Akimori's father. Akimori was also one of Fenton's pupils. Although the melody is based on a traditional mode of Japanese court music, it is composed in a mixed style influenced by Western hymns, and uses some elements of the Fenton arrangement.Hermann Gottschewski: "''Hoiku shōka'' and the melody of the Japanese national anthem ''Kimi ga yo''", in: ''Journal of the Society for Research in Asiatic Music'' (東洋音楽研究), No. 68 (2003), pp. 1–17. Published by [http://wwwsoc.nii.ac.jp/tog/ The society for Research in Asiatic Music] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090211083829/http://wwwsoc.nii.ac.jp/tog/|date=2009-02-11}} The German musician {{ill|Franz Eckert|en|Franz Eckert|WD=Q569367|lt=Franz Eckert|1=Franz Eckert}} applied the melody with Western style harmony, creating the second and current version of "Kimigayo". The government formally adopted "Kimigayo" as the national anthem in 1888 and had copies of the music and lyrics sent overseas for diplomatic ceremonies.{{cite book|last1=Boyd|first1=Richard|last2=Ngo|first2=Tak-Wing|title=State Making in Asia|publisher=Routledge|year=2006|page=36|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=r8IDxzZ4SQIC&q=kimigayo&pg=PA36|access-date=2010-10-14|isbn=978-0-415-34611-5|archive-date=2024-02-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240229221403/https://books.google.com/books?id=r8IDxzZ4SQIC&q=kimigayo&pg=PA36#v=snippet&q=kimigayo&f=false|url-status=live}} By 1893, "Kimigayo" was included in public school ceremonies due to the efforts of the then [[:en:Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (Japan)|Ministry of Education]]. [[File:Kimigayo-Anthem-Japan-Sheet-Music-1888.png|thumb|Kimigayo sheet music, 1888]] Kōzō Yoshimoto (吉本光蔵, 1863–1907) [[[:ja:吉本光藏|ja]]] composed the Kimigayo March (君が代行進曲) [[[:ja:君が代行進曲|ja]]] based on the anthem and another composition called ''Defense of the Japanese Empire'' (皇国の守り) by {{ill|Isawa Shūji|en|Isawa Shūji|WD=Q10885047|lt=Isawa Shūji|1=Isawa Shūji}}. The march is still performed by the {{ill|Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force|en|Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force|WD=Q731647|lt=Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force|1=Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force}} band.{{Citation |title=Kimigayo March - Japanese Navy Band | date=27 May 2018 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9pldWsWV320 |language=en |access-date=2023-02-10 |archive-date=2023-02-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230210222545/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9pldWsWV320&gl=US&hl=en |url-status=live }} At the turn of the 20th century, "Kimigayo" was beginning to be closely associated with the idea of honoring the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor|1=Emperor of Japan}}. It was also associated as a part of Japanese education. However, opinions expressed in an Osaka paper in 1904 calls "Kimigayo" a song for the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=imperial family|1=Imperial House of Japan}} and not the state as a whole.{{sfn|Goodman|Neary|1996|p=79}} [[:en:Uchimura Kanzo|Uchimura Kanzo]], a Christian leader in Japan, stated at the turn of the 20th century that "Kimigayo" is not the anthem of Japan by saying the song's purpose is to praise the emperor. According to Kanzo, a national anthem should express the feelings of the people, and not of the divine emperor.{{cite book|last1=Shields|first1=James J. Jr.|title=Japanese Schooling: Patterns of Socialization, Equality, and Political Control|publisher=Penn State University Press|year=1989|page=241|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ssHlZQvhOA4C&q=kimigayo+Kakuei&pg=PA241|access-date=2010-10-14|isbn=978-0-271-02340-3|archive-date=2024-02-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240229221422/https://books.google.com/books?id=ssHlZQvhOA4C&q=kimigayo+Kakuei&pg=PA241#v=snippet&q=kimigayo%20Kakuei&f=false|url-status=live}} The Japanese were not familiar with "Kimigayo" as the anthem until there was a surge of celebrations after victories in the {{ill|First Sino-Japanese War|en|First Sino-Japanese War|WD=Q178687|lt=First Sino-Japanese|1=First Sino-Japanese War}} and {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|en|Russo-Japanese War|WD=Q159950|lt=Russo-Japanese War|1=Russo-Japanese War}}s. Previously, papers were critical of fellow Japanese who could not sing "Kimigayo" properly at ceremonies overseas. During {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War|1=Pacific War}}, the {{ill|Empire of Japan|en|Empire of Japan|WD=Q188712|lt=Japanese Empire|1=Empire of Japan}} ordered that schoolchildren, both from its homeland and {{ill|Japanese colonial empire|en|Japanese colonial empire|WD=Q6158424|lt=its colonies|1=Japanese colonial empire}}, were to sing the "Kimigayo" anthem and salute Emperor {{ill|Hirohito|en|Hirohito|WD=Q34479|lt=Hirohito|1=Hirohito}} every morning. === Postwar Japan (1945–present) === ==== 1945 to 1999 ==== During the {{ill|Occupation of Japan|en|Occupation of Japan|WD=Q696251|lt=Allied occupation of Japan|1=Occupation of Japan}} (led mainly by the {{ill|United States|en|United States|WD=Q30|lt=United States|1=United States}}), there were no directives by the [[Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers]] to restrict the use of "Kimigayo" by the [[Government of Japan|Japanese government]]. This was different from the regulations issued that restricted the use of the ''{{ill|Flag of Japan|en|Flag of Japan|WD=Q43175|lt=Hinomaru|1=Flag of Japan}}'' flag.{{sfn|Goodman|Neary|1996|p=81}} Along with the encouragement to use "Kimigayo" in the schools to promote defense education and {{ill|Patriotism|en|Patriotism|WD=Q6241|lt=Patriotism|1=Patriotism}}, the national broadcaster {{ill|NHK|en|NHK|WD=Q212128|lt=NHK|1=NHK}} began to use the song to announce the start and ending of its programming.{{sfn|Goodman|Neary|1996|p=82}} ==== Since 1999 ==== [[File:国旗及び国歌に関する法律.jpg|thumb|alt=A page with Asian characters and a black-and-white version of the Japanese flag left above|The ''Act on National Flag and Anthem (Japan)'' as it appears in the Official Gazette on 15 August 1999]] The "{{ill|Act on National Flag and Anthem|en|Act on National Flag and Anthem|WD=Q3270407|lt=Act on National Flag and Anthem|1=Act on National Flag and Anthem}}" was passed on 13 August 1999, choosing both the ''Hinomaru'' and "Kimigayo" as Japan's national symbols. The passage of the law stemmed from a suicide of a school principal in Hiroshima who could not resolve a dispute between his school board and his teachers over the use of the ''Hinomaru'' and "Kimigayo".{{sfn|Aspinall|2001|p=126}} {{ill|Prime Minister of Japan|en|Prime Minister of Japan|WD=Q274948|lt=Prime Minister|1=Prime Minister of Japan}} {{ill|Keizō Obuchi|en|Keizō Obuchi|WD=Q313339|lt=Keizō Obuchi|1=Keizō Obuchi}}, President of the {{ill|Liberal Democratic Party (Japan)|en|Liberal Democratic Party (Japan)|WD=Q232595|lt=Liberal Democratic Party|1=Liberal Democratic Party (Japan)}} (LDP) decided to draft legislation to make the ''Hinomaru'' and "Kimigayo" official symbols of Japan in 2000. His {{ill|Chief Cabinet Secretary|en|Chief Cabinet Secretary|WD=Q1078482|lt=Chief Cabinet Secretary|1=Chief Cabinet Secretary}}, {{ill|Hiromu Nonaka|en|Hiromu Nonaka|WD=Q696583|lt=Hiromu Nonaka|1=Hiromu Nonaka}}, wanted the legislation to be completed by the 10th anniversary of the coronation of {{ill|Akihito|en|Akihito|WD=Q37979|lt=Akihito|1=Akihito}} as Emperor.{{sfn|Itoh|2003|pp=209–210}} This is not the first time legislation was considered for establishing both symbols as official. In 1974, with the backdrop of the {{ill|1971 Okinawa Reversion Agreement|en|1971 Okinawa Reversion Agreement|WD=Q11553006|lt=1972 return of Okinawa Prefecture|1=1971 Okinawa Reversion Agreement}} to Japan from the U.S. and the {{ill|1973 oil crisis|en|1973 oil crisis|WD=Q316817|lt=1973 oil crisis|1=1973 oil crisis}}, Prime Minister {{ill|Kakuei Tanaka|en|Kakuei Tanaka|WD=Q297644|lt=Kakuei Tanaka|1=Kakuei Tanaka}} hinted at a law being passed legalizing both symbols.{{sfn|Goodman|Neary|1996|pp=82–83}} The main supporters of the bill were governing parties, the LDP and the {{ill|Komeito|en|Komeito|WD=Q1061354|lt=Komeito|1=Komeito}} (CGP), while the opposition included the {{ill|Social Democratic Party (Japan)|en|Social Democratic Party (Japan)|WD=Q835109|lt=Social Democratic Party|1=Social Democratic Party (Japan)}} (SDPJ) and {{ill|Japanese Communist Party|en|Japanese Communist Party|WD=Q641600|lt=Communist Party|1=Japanese Communist Party}} (JCP), who cited the connotations both symbols had with the war era. The JCP was further opposed for not allowing the issue to be decided by the public. Meanwhile, the {{ill|Democratic Party of Japan|en|Democratic Party of Japan|WD=Q200314|lt=Democratic Party of Japan|1=Democratic Party of Japan}} (DPJ) could not develop party consensus on it. President of the DPJ and future prime minister, {{ill|Naoto Kan|en|Naoto Kan|WD=Q47846|lt=Naoto Kan|1=Naoto Kan}} stated that the DPJ must support the bill because the party already recognized both symbols as the symbols of Japan.{{cite web |url=http://www.dpj.or.jp/news/?num=11044 |title=国旗国歌法制化についての民主党の考え方 |access-date=2010-01-17 |date=1999-07-21 |publisher=Democratic Party of Japan |trans-title=The DPJ Asks For A Talk About the Flag and Anthem Law |language=ja |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110728091749/http://www.dpj.or.jp/news/?num=11044 |archive-date=July 28, 2011 }} Deputy Secretary General and future prime minister {{ill|Yukio Hatoyama|en|Yukio Hatoyama|WD=Q131077|lt=Yukio Hatoyama|1=Yukio Hatoyama}} thought that this bill would cause further divisions among society and the public schools.{{sfn|Itoh|2003|pp=209–210}} Before the vote, there were calls for the bills to be separated at the {{ill|National Diet|en|National Diet|WD=Q202384|lt=National Diet|1=National Diet}}. {{ill|Waseda University|en|Waseda University|WD=Q274486|lt=Waseda University|1=Waseda University}} professor Norihiro Kato stated that "Kimigayo" is a separate issue more complex than the ''Hinomaru'' flag.{{sfn|Calichman|2005|p=211}} Attempts to designate only the ''Hinomaru'' as the national flag by the DPJ and other parties during the vote of the bill were rejected by the Diet.{{cite web |url=http://www.dpj.or.jp/news/?num=8506 |title=国旗・国歌法案、衆院で可決 民主党は自主投票 |access-date=2010-01-18 |trans-title=Flag and Anthem Law Passed by the House, DPJ Free Vote|date=1999-07-22 |publisher=Democratic Party of Japan |language=ja|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110728091823/http://www.dpj.or.jp/news/?num=8506 |archive-date=July 28, 2011 |url-status=dead}} The House of Representatives passed the bill on July 22, 1999, by a 403 to 86 vote.{{cite web |url=http://kokkai.ndl.go.jp/SENTAKU/syugiin/145/0001/14507220001047c.html|title=第１４５回国会 本会議 第４７号|access-date=2010-01-17|date=1999-07-22|publisher=National Diet Library|language=ja|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120714043020/http://kokkai.ndl.go.jp/SENTAKU/syugiin/145/0001/14507220001047c.html |archive-date=2012-07-14|url-status=dead}} The legislation was sent to the House of Councilors on July 28 and was passed on August 9. It was enacted into law on August 13.{{cite web |url=http://www.shugiin.go.jp/itdb_gian.nsf/html/gian/keika/1CE3AB6.htm|title=議案審議経過情報: 国旗及び国歌に関する法律案 |access-date=2010-01-17|date=1999-08-13|publisher=House of Representatives|language=ja |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110323180056/http://www.shugiin.go.jp/itdb_gian.nsf/html/gian/keika/1CE3AB6.htm |archive-date=2011-03-23 |url-status=dead}} == Protocol == [[File:Kimi ga Yo at volleyball tournament.jpg|thumb|upright=1.15|A photo taken on November 6, 2007, as "Kimigayo" was being played before a volleyball tournament in {{ill|Osaka|en|Osaka|WD=Q35765|lt=Ōsaka|1=Osaka}}]] The lyrics and {{ill|musical notation|en|musical notation|WD=Q233861|lt=musical notation|1=Musical notation}} of the anthem are given in the second appendix of the {{ill|Act on National Flag and Anthem|en|Act on National Flag and Anthem|WD=Q3270407|lt=Act on National Flag and Anthem|1=Act on National Flag and Anthem}}. As for the sheet music itself, it displays a vocal arrangement with no mention of tempo and all of the lyrics in {{ill|Hiragana|en|Hiragana|WD=Q48332|lt=Hiragana|1=Hiragana}}. The anthem is composed in 4/4 ({{ill|Time signature|en|Time signature|WD=Q155234|lt=common time|1=Time signature}}) in the {{ill|Dorian mode|en|Dorian mode|WD=Q960729|lt=Dorian mode|1=Dorian mode}}.{{cite web|title=国旗及び国歌に関する法律（平成十一年法律第百二十七号）|trans-title=Act on National Flag and Anthem, Act No. 127 in the 11th year of [[Heisei era|Heisei]] (1999)|url=https://elaws.e-gov.go.jp/document?lawid=411AC0000000127|access-date=30 March 2021|date=13 August 1999|publisher=[[Government of Japan]]|language=ja|archive-date=4 June 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230604022952/https://elaws.e-gov.go.jp/document?lawid=411AC0000000127|url-status=live}} The {{ill|Act on National Flag and Anthem|en|Act on National Flag and Anthem|WD=Q3270407|lt=Act on National Flag and Anthem|1=Act on National Flag and Anthem}} does not detail how one should show respect during performances of "Kimigayo". In a statement made by Prime Minister Obuchi, the legislation will not impose new regulations on the Japanese people when it comes to respecting the flag or anthem.{{cite web|url=http://www.mofa.go.jp/announce/announce/1999/8/809.html|title=Statement of Prime Minister Keizo Obuchi|access-date=2010-05-17|date=1999-08-09|publisher=Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan|archive-date=2011-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110524023306/http://www.mofa.go.jp/announce/announce/1999/8/809.html|url-status=live}} However, local government bodies and private organizations sometimes suggest or demand certain protocols be followed. For example, an October 2003 directive by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government required teachers to stand during the national anthem at graduation ceremonies. While standing, the teachers are required to sing "Kimigayo" while facing the {{ill|Flag of Japan|en|Flag of Japan|WD=Q43175|lt=''Hinomaru''|1=Flag of Japan}}.{{cite web|date=2004-04-07|url=http://search.japantimes.co.jp/cgi-bin/ed20040407a1.html|title=Editorial: Coercion can't foster respect|work={{ill|The Japan Times|en|The Japan Times|WD=Q1190886|lt=The Japan Times|1=The Japan Times}} Online|access-date=2007-12-19|archive-date=2012-05-26|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120526023147/http://www.japantimes.co.jp/text/ed20040407a1.html|url-status=live}} The Act on National Flag and Anthem also does not dictate when or where "Kimigayo" should be played. The anthem, however, is commonly played at sporting events inside of Japan, or at international sporting events where Japan has a competing team. At {{ill|Sumo|en|Sumo|WD=Q40561|lt=''sumō''|1=Sumo}} tournaments, "Kimigayo" is played before the awards ceremony. === Public schools === Since the {{ill|End of World War II in Asia|en|End of World War II in Asia|WD=Q5375854|lt=end of World War II|1=End of World War II in Asia}}, the [[:en:Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (Japan)|Ministry of Education]] has issued statements and regulations to promote the usage of both the ''Hinomaru'' and "Kimigayo" at schools under their jurisdiction. The first of these statements was released in 1950, stating that it was desirable, but not required, to use both symbols. This desire was later expanded to include both symbols on national holidays and during ceremonial events to encourage students on what national holidays are and to promote defense education. The Ministry not only took great measures to explain that both symbols are not formally established by law, they also referred to "Kimigayo" as a song and refused to call it the national anthem. It was not until 1977 that the Ministry referred to {{nihongo|"Kimigayo"|君が代}} as the {{nihongo|national anthem|国歌|kokka}} of Japan.{{sfn|Goodman|Neary|1996|pp=81–83}} In a 1989 reform of the education guidelines, the LDP-controlled government first demanded that the ''Hinomaru'' flag must be used in school ceremonies and that proper respect must be given to it and to "Kimigayo".{{sfn|Trevor|2001|p=78}} Punishments for school officials who did not follow this order were also enacted with the 1989 reforms.{{sfn|Goodman|Neary|1996|pp=81–83}} The 1999 [[:en:curriculum guideline|curriculum guideline]] issued by the {{ill|Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology|en|Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology|WD=Q1054379|lt=Ministry of Education|1=Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology}} after the passage of the ''{{ill|Act on National Flag and Anthem|en|Act on National Flag and Anthem|WD=Q3270407|lt=Law Regarding the National Flag and Anthem|1=Act on National Flag and Anthem}}'' decrees that "on entrance and graduation ceremonies, schools must raise the flag of Japan and instruct students to sing the "Kimigayo" (national anthem), given the significance of the flag and the song."{{cite web |url=http://www.pref.hiroshima.lg.jp/kyouiku/hotline/02zesei/sankou/kokkikokka.htm |title=学習指導要領における国旗及び国歌の取扱い |trans-title=Handling of the flag and anthem in the National Curriculum|access-date=2009-12-08 |date=2001-09-11|publisher=Hiroshima Prefectural Board of Education Secretariat|language=ja|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110722112237/http://www.pref.hiroshima.lg.jp/kyouiku/hotline/02zesei/sankou/kokkikokka.htm |archive-date=2011-07-22 }} Additionally, the ministry's commentary on 1999 curriculum guideline for elementary schools note that "given the advance of internationalization, along with fostering patriotism and awareness of being Japanese, it is important to nurture school children's respectful attitude toward the flag of Japan and "Kimigayo" as they grow up to be respected Japanese citizens in an internationalized society."{{cite web|title=小学校学習指導要領解説社会編，音楽編，特別活動編 |trans-title=National Curriculum Guide: Elementary social notes, Chapter music Chapter Special Activities |publisher=Ministry of Education |language=ja |year=1999 |url=http://cebc.jp/data/education/gov/jp/tsuuchi/19990917hatauta/data-02.htm |url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060319210723/http://cebc.jp/data/education/gov/jp/tsuuchi/19990917hatauta/data-02.htm |archive-date=2006-03-19}} The ministry also stated that if Japanese students cannot respect their own symbols, then they will not be able to respect the symbols of other nations.{{sfn|Aspinall|2001|p=125}} == Present-day perception == According to a survey conducted by {{ill|TV Asahi|en|TV Asahi|WD=Q908436|lt=TV Asahi|1=TV Asahi}}, most {{ill|Japanese people|en|Japanese people|WD=Q161652|lt=Japanese people|1=Japanese people}} perceived "Kimigayo" as an important, yet a controversial song even before the passage of the ''{{ill|Act on National Flag and Anthem|en|Act on National Flag and Anthem|WD=Q3270407|lt=Act on National Flag and Anthem|1=Act on National Flag and Anthem}}'' in 1999.{{cite web |url=http://www.tv-asahi.co.jp/n-station/research/990717/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080523125535/http://www.tv-asahi.co.jp/n-station/research/990717/index.html|archive-date=2008-05-23|title=国旗・国歌法制化について|trans-title=About the Law of the Flag and Anthem|work=Asahi Research|publisher=TV Asahi|language=ja |date=1999-07-18 |access-date=2008-03-11}} However, a poll in the same year, conducted by the Mainichi Shimbun, found that most respondents opposed legislation that make it the national anthem, or thought that the Diet should take more time in passing such a law.{{cite web |url=http://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/1999/08/09/national/flag-anthem-law-no-end-to-controversy/ |author=Asako Murakami |title=Flag-anthem law no end to controversy |work={{ill|The Japan Times|en|The Japan Times|WD=Q1190886|lt=The Japan Times|1=The Japan Times}} Online |date=1999-08-09 |access-date=2015-12-21 |url-access=subscription |archive-date=2022-04-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220421171822/https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/1999/08/09/national/flag-anthem-law-no-end-to-controversy/ |url-status=live }} Many Japanese students, who must sing the song at entrance and graduation ceremonies, say they cannot understand the old and obsolete language of the lyrics and are not educated on its historical uses.{{cite web |author=Mayumi Negishi |title='Kimigayo' controversy leaves students indifferent, confused |work={{ill|The Japan Times|en|The Japan Times|WD=Q1190886|lt=The Japan Times|1=The Japan Times}} Online |date=1999-07-09 |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/1999/07/22/national/kimigayo-controversy-leaves-students-indifferent-confused/ |access-date=2015-12-21 |url-access=subscription |archive-date=2023-04-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230404165511/https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/1999/07/22/national/kimigayo-controversy-leaves-students-indifferent-confused/ |url-status=live }} Controversies surrounding the use of the anthem in school events still remain. == Lyrics == === Japanese original === {|class="wikitable" rules="cols" Japanese|WD=Q192509|lt=Rōmaji|1=Romanization of Japanese}} !{{ill|International Phonetic Alphabet|en|International Phonetic Alphabet|WD=Q21204|lt=IPA|1=International Phonetic Alphabet}} !Poetic English translation
by {{ill|Basil Hall Chamberlain|en|Basil Hall Chamberlain|WD=Q810029|lt=Basil Hall Chamberlain|1=Basil Hall Chamberlain}}{{cite web|title=Politika i ekonomija (Upoznajte Japan) |url=http://www.yu.emb-japan.go.jp/Srpski/UpoznajteJapan-PolitikaEkonomija.htm |access-date=2010-05-17 |year=2003 |publisher=Japanska ambasada u Srbiji i Crnoj Gori |language=sr |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100428014321/http://www.yu.emb-japan.go.jp/Srpski/UpoznajteJapan-PolitikaEkonomija.htm |archive-date=2010-04-28|url-status=dead}} |- style="vertical-align:top; white-space:nowrap;" |May {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=your reign|1=Emperor of Japan}} Continue for a thousand, [[8#As a lucky number|eight]] thousand generations, Until the tiny pebbles Grow into massive boulders Lush with [[moss]] |Thousands of years of happy reign be thine; Rule on, {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=my lord|1=Emperor of Japan}}, until what are pebbles now By ages united to mighty rocks shall grow Whose venerable sides the moss doth line. |} == Controversies == Japan's national anthem is controversial due to its {{ill|Postwar Japan|en|Postwar Japan|WD=Q1046461|lt=post-war history|1=Postwar Japan}}.{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GeasCAAAQBAJ |title=Republic or Death! Travels in Search of National Anthems|last=Marshall |first=Alex|publisher=Windmill Books |year=2016|isbn=978-0-09-959223-5|location=London|pages=99–100|quote="All anthems stir up controversy at some point...But no matter how heated such controversies get, none comes close to that around Kimigayo. It's a conflict that's been going on in Japan's schools for over 70 years. Teachers have lost jobs because of it. They've received death threats because of it. Parents have been left dazed by it, worrying about their children's future. And yes, Toshihiro Ishikawa committed suicide because of it."}} {{ill|Education in Japan|en|Education in Japan|WD=Q834934|lt=Schools|1=Education in Japan}} have been the center of controversy over both it and the national flag.{{cite news |author=Weisman, Steven R. |title=For Japanese, Flag and Anthem Sometimes Divide |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/04/29/world/for-japanese-flag-and-anthem-sometimes-divide.html#end_copy |work=The New York Times |date=1990-04-29 |access-date=2010-01-02 |archive-date=2013-05-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130524130632/http://www.nytimes.com/1990/04/29/world/for-japanese-flag-and-anthem-sometimes-divide.html#end_copy |url-status=live }} The Tokyo Board of Education requires the use of both "Kimigayo" and flag at events under their jurisdiction. The order requires school teachers to respect both symbols or risk losing their jobs.{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2006/jun/05/worlddispatch.japan|title=A touchy subject|publisher=Guardian Unlimited|work=The Guardian|author=McCurry, Justin|date=2006-06-05|access-date=2008-01-14|archive-date=2012-10-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121029123404/http://www.guardian.co.uk/world/2006/jun/05/worlddispatch.japan|url-status=live}} In 1999, several teachers in {{ill|Hiroshima|en|Hiroshima|WD=Q34664|lt=Hiroshima|1=Hiroshima}} refused to put up the anthem while the Hiroshima Education Board demanded that they do so. As the tension arose between them, a vice-principal killed himself. A similar incident in Osaka in 2010 also occurred, with 32 teachers refusing to sing the song in a ceremony. In 2011, nine more teachers joined the rebellion, along with another eight in 2012.{{cite web |title=8 Osaka teachers to be punished for refusal to sing national anthem |url=http://www.japantoday.com/Category:11]] [[Category/national/view/8-osaka-teachers-face-punishment-over-refusal-to-sing-national-anthem |website=Japan Today |date=25 February 2012 |access-date=February 25, 2012 |archive-date=16 June 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160616230835/http://www.japantoday.com/Category:11]] [[Category/national/view/8-osaka-teachers-face-punishment-over-refusal-to-sing-national-anthem |url-status=live }} [[:en:Hashimoto Toru|Hashimoto Toru]], the mayor of {{ill|Osaka|en|Osaka|WD=Q35765|lt=Osaka|1=Osaka}}, stated that "[i]t was good that criminals who are intent on breaking the rules have risen to the surface".{{cite web |title=Teachers Who Refused To Sing National Anthem Face Punishment |website=japanCRUSH |publisher=Beth |url=http://www.japancrush.com/2013/stories/teachers-who-refused-to-sing-national-anthem-face-punishment.html |access-date=March 6, 2013 |archive-date=April 21, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220421171830/https://www.japancrush.com/2013/stories/teachers-who-refused-to-sing-national-anthem-face-punishment.html |url-status=live }} Some have protested that such rules violate the {{ill|United Nations|en|United Nations|WD=Q1065|lt=United Nations|1=United Nations}} {{ill|Universal Declaration of Human Rights|en|Universal Declaration of Human Rights|WD=Q7813|lt=Universal Declaration of Human Rights|1=Universal Declaration of Human Rights}} and the "freedom of thought, belief and conscience" clause in the {{ill|Constitution of Japan|en|Constitution of Japan|WD=Q237082|lt=Constitution of Japan|1=Constitution of Japan}},{{cite book |last1=Grossman |last2=Lee |first2=Wing On |last3=Kennedy |first3=Kerry |title=Citizenship Curriculum in Asia and the Pacific |publisher=Springer |year=2008 |page=85 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=btkuYUgXLRIC&q=kimigayo&pg=PA85|access-date=2010-10-12 |isbn=978-1-4020-8744-8}} but the Board has argued that since schools are government agencies, their employees have an obligation to teach their students how to be good Japanese citizens. Teachers have unsuccessfully brought criminal complaints against {{ill|Governor of Tokyo|en|Governor of Tokyo|WD=Q11525354|lt=Governor of Tokyo|1=Governor of Tokyo}} [[:en:Shintarō Ishihara|Shintarō Ishihara]] and senior officials for ordering teachers to honour the ''Hinomaru'' and "Kimigayo".{{cite web|url=http://search.japantimes.co.jp/cgi-bin/nn20060105b2.html|title=Ishihara's Hinomaru order called legit|work={{ill|The Japan Times|en|The Japan Times|WD=Q1190886|lt=The Japan Times|1=The Japan Times}} Online|date=2006-01-05|access-date=2007-12-04|archive-date=2012-12-27|archive-url=https://archive.today/20121227215302/http://www.japantimes.co.jp/text/nn20060105b2.html|url-status=live}} After earlier opposition, the {{ill|Japan Teachers Union|en|Japan Teachers Union|WD=Q843872|lt=Japan Teachers Union|1=Japan Teachers Union}} accepts the use of both the flag and national anthem; the smaller All Japan Teachers and Staffs Union still opposes both symbols and their use inside the school system.{{sfn|Heenan|1998|p=206}} In 2006, Katsuhisa Fujita, a retired teacher in {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|WD=Q1490|lt=Tokyo|1=Tokyo}}, was threatened with {{ill|imprisonment|en|imprisonment|WD=Q841236|lt=imprisonment|1=Imprisonment}} and fined 200,000 {{ill|Japanese yen|en|Japanese yen|WD=Q8146|lt=yen|1=Japanese yen}} (roughly 2,000 {{ill|United States dollar|en|United States dollar|WD=Q4917|lt=US dollars|1=United States dollar}}) after he was accused of disturbing a {{ill|graduation|en|graduation|WD=Q1054021|lt=graduation|1=Graduation}} ceremony at {{ill|Itabashi|en|Itabashi|WD=Q232635|lt=Itabashi|1=Itabashi}} {{ill|Secondary school|en|Secondary school|WD=Q159334|lt=Senior High School|1=Secondary school}} by urging the attendees to remain seated during the playing of the national anthem.{{cite web |date = 2006-05-24 |url = http://home.kyodo.co.jp/modules/fstStory/index.php?storyid=248658 |title = Feature: Upcoming verdict on retired teacher draws attention |work = Kyodo News On The Web |access-date = 2006-07-29 |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060618201400/http://home.kyodo.co.jp/modules/fstStory/index.php?storyid=248658 |archive-date = 2006-06-18 }} At the time of Fujita's sentence, 345 teachers had been punished for refusing to take part in anthem related events, though Fujita is the only man to have been convicted in relation to it.{{cite news | title = Japanese teacher fined for anthem protest | date = 2006-05-31 | publisher = AFP | url = http://www.taipeitimes.com/News/world/archives/2006/05/31/2003310932 | work = [[The Taipei Times]] | access-date = 2010-10-14 | archive-date = 2022-08-30 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20220830142736/https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/world/archives/2006/05/31/2003310932 | url-status = live }} On 21 September 2006, the Tokyo District Court ordered the Tokyo Metropolitan Government to pay compensation to the teachers who had been subjected to punishment under the directive of the Tokyo Board of Education. The then {{ill|Prime Minister of Japan|en|Prime Minister of Japan|WD=Q274948|lt=Prime Minister|1=Prime Minister of Japan}} {{ill|Junichiro Koizumi|en|Junichiro Koizumi|WD=Q130852|lt=Junichiro Koizumi|1=Junichiro Koizumi}} commented, "It is a natural idea to treat the national anthem importantly". The ruling was appealed by the Metropolitan Government.{{cite web |date=2006-09-23 |url=http://search.japantimes.co.jp/cgi-bin/nn20060923a2.html |title=City Hall to appeal 'Kimigayo' ruling |work={{ill|The Japan Times|en|The Japan Times|WD=Q1190886|lt=The Japan Times|1=The Japan Times}} Online |access-date=2007-10-25 |archive-date=2012-05-26 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120526023233/search.japantimes.co.jp/cgi-bin/nn20060923a2.html |url-status=live }} From 23 October 2003 to 2008, 410 teachers and school workers were punished for refusing to stand and sing the anthem as ordered by school principals.{{cite news |title=2 teachers punished for refusing to stand up, recite 'Kimigayo' |date=2008-05-24 |url=http://www.japantoday.com/Category:11]] [[Category/national/view/2-teachers-punished-for-refusing-to-stand-up-recite-kimigayo |archive-url=http://arquivo.pt/wayback/20091015193543/http://www.japantoday.com/Category:11]] [[Category/national/view/2-teachers-punished-for-refusing-to-stand-up-recite-kimigayo |url-status=dead |archive-date=2009-10-15 |work=Kyodo News |publisher=Japan Today |access-date=2010-10-14}} Teachers can also be punished if their students do not stand while "Kimigayo" is played during school ceremonies. On 30 May 2011 and 6 June 2011, two panels of the {{ill|Supreme Court of Japan|en|Supreme Court of Japan|WD=Q1142255|lt=Supreme Court of Japan|1=Supreme Court of Japan}} ruled that it was constitutional to require teachers to stand in front of the {{ill|Flag of Japan|en|Flag of Japan|WD=Q43175|lt=Hinomaru|1=Flag of Japan}} and sing the Kimigayo during school ceremonies. In making the ruling, the panels ratified the decision of the {{ill|Tokyo High Court|en|Tokyo High Court|WD=Q82679|lt=Tokyo High Court|1=Tokyo High Court}} in ruling against 13 teachers who had asked for court relief after being disciplined between 2003 and 2005 for refusing to stand and sing the anthem.{{cite web|author=Kyodo News|title=Top court again backs 'Kimigayo' orders|url=http://search.japantimes.co.jp/cgi-bin/nn20110608b1.html|work={{ill|The Japan Times|en|The Japan Times|WD=Q1190886|lt=The Japan Times|1=The Japan Times}} Online|access-date=15 October 2011|archive-date=21 August 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110821231030/http://search.japantimes.co.jp/cgi-bin/nn20110608b1.html|url-status=live}} Outside of the school system, there was a controversy regarding "Kimigayo" soon after the passage of the 1999 law. A month after the law's passage, a record containing a performance of "Kimigayo" by Japanese rock musician {{ill|Kiyoshiro Imawano|en|Kiyoshiro Imawano|WD=Q1041744|lt=Kiyoshiro Imawano|1=Kiyoshiro Imawano}} was removed by Polydor Records from his album ''Fuyu no Jujika'' (冬の十字架, ''Cross in Winter''). Polydor did not want to attract harassment from {{ill|Uyoku dantai|en|Uyoku dantai|WD=Q181924|lt=far-right groups|1=Uyoku dantai}}. In response, Imawano re-released the album through an independent label with the track in question.{{cite magazine |first=Steve |last=McClure |date=1999-09-25 |title=Polydor Censors Japanese Rocker |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cAgEAAAAMBAJ&q=Kimigayo&pg=PA73 |magazine=Billboard |page=73 |access-date=2009-08-25}} == See also == {{Portal|Music|Japan}} {{Column list| * [[:en:Imperial Seal by {{ill|Franz Eckert|en|Franz Eckert|WD=Q569367|lt=Franz Eckert|1=Franz Eckert}}) }} | music_date = 1880 | adopted = {{Plain list| * 1869 (original music) * 1870 (lyrics) * 3 November 1880 (current
